edges.effect_quant: A 2021 dose-response meta-analysis reported a pooled risk ratio of 1.11 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.15) for highest versus lowest light-at-night exposure. In the French E3N nested case-control analysis, each interquartile-range increase in outdoor LAN was associated with an OR of 1.11 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.20). In a 24,793-woman pooled cohort, the highest tertile of melatonin-suppressive outdoor light was associated with a 1.53-fold higher breast cancer hazard among women reporting light entering the bedroom, but the overall cohort estimate was null.
edges.population: adult women exposed chronically to outdoor artificial light at night
edges.mechanism: Nighttime light can suppress melatonin and shift circadian timing, which may alter estrogen signaling, cell-cycle control, and DNA repair in breast tissue. The signal appears strongest when light intensity, spectrum, and actual nighttime bedroom exposure line up rather than from outdoor brightness alone.
edges.summary: The literature supports a cautious harmful reading, but not a dramatic one. The strongest takeaway is that chronic light-at-night exposure probably contributes a small breast-cancer risk signal that becomes more convincing in studies with better exposure characterization, while some large cohorts still attenuate toward null after adjustment for urban co-exposures.
edges.caveats: This edge is sensitive to confounding by urbanicity, air pollution, greenness, and indoor nighttime light behavior. It is also possible that wavelength and bedroom penetration matter more than outdoor brightness alone, so the exposure is still measured imperfectly in many cohorts.
